strengths: Provides closed-form variance-preserving initialization derivations for orthogonal basis activations (Hermite, Fourier), addressing a genuine gap left by prior rational-activation work that had to rely on function-fitting tricks.

Evaluates on genuinely large-scale tasks (ImageNet-1k with ConvNeXt-T, OpenWebText with GPT-2 124M) rather than toy benchmarks like MNIST, which the paper itself (rightly) criticizes much of the KAN-inspired literature for using.
Includes a reasonably thorough set of ablations (degree, initialization scheme, learnability of coefficients, clamping) that support the individual design choices.
Formalizes the connection between polynomial activations and polynomial/tropical mappings, situating the work within existing theory (Zhang et al. 2018, Kileel et al. 2019).

Attention to practical implementation details (numerically stable Hermite recurrence, custom CUDA-style kernels, FLOPs/memory complexity discussion) adds some engineering value and reproducibility potential.
weaknesses: Empirical results are based on single training runs with no reported variance across seeds despite claims of 'fixed random seeds to ensure reproducibility'; the improvements reported (e.g., GPT-2 val loss 2.9571→2.9119, ConvNeXt top-1 82.04→82.34) are small and could plausibly fall within run-to-run noise.

Results are mixed rather than uniformly positive: Fourier activation actually underperforms the GELU baseline on ImageNet-1k (81.91% vs 82.04% top-1, 95.77% vs 96.01% top-5), which contradicts the paper's framing that the proposed activations 'significantly improve' over baselines.

No direct empirical comparison against the closely related rational activation approach of Yang & Wang (2024), which is repeatedly referenced as the key prior work motivating this paper; without this baseline it's hard to assess whether polynomial/trigonometric activations are actually preferable to rational ones in practice.
Only one model size is tested per modality (ConvNeXt-T, GPT-2-124M), limiting claims about scalability of the approach to 'large-scale' or deeper networks in general.

No evidence is shown that networks without the proposed initialization actually fail to converge/diverge (e.g., loss curves under naive initialization); Table 4 only compares two different working initializations rather than demonstrating an instability failure mode, weakening the core motivating claim about vanishing/exploding gradients.

Tropical activations are not covered by the variance-preserving theory (deferred to future work), yet they are included in the main experimental claims, creating a mismatch between the theoretical contribution and the empirical scope of the abstract.

Practical overhead (wall-clock training/inference time, real memory footprint) is discussed only in asymptotic complexity terms (O(d), O(d^2)) without concrete measurements, making it hard to judge whether the accuracy/perplexity gains justify the added computational cost.

The paper is somewhat unfocused, with substantial space devoted to tangential discussions (e.g., the KAN/Kolmogorov-Arnold digression in the appendix, extensive related work) that dilute the presentation of the core contribution and experimental analysis.

strengths: Provides a rigorous, closed-form theoretical derivation of variance-preserving initialization for orthogonal-basis (Hermite, Fourier) learnable activations, extending the He et al. (2015) framework in a principled way that avoids the curve-fitting trick used in prior rational-activation work (Yang & Wang, 2024).

Tests learnable activations on genuinely large-scale tasks (ImageNet-1K with ConvNeXt-T, OpenWebText with GPT-2), which is a meaningful departure from much of the cited KAN/learnable-activation literature that only validates on toy datasets like MNIST.
Includes ablation studies varying activation degree, learnability of coefficients, and initialization scheme, which help isolate the contribution of each design choice.

Careful attention to practical/numerical implementation issues (stable power computation, recursive Hermite formulas, custom kernels, FLOPs/memory complexity analysis) that would matter for real adoption.
Extensive and well-organized related-work survey connecting KAN, tropical geometry, and orthogonal polynomial literature.
weaknesses: Experiments appear to be single-run (fixed seed) with no repeated trials, confidence intervals, or variance estimates; the reported gains are small (e.g., ConvNeXt top-1: 82.04% baseline vs 82.34% Hermite, a 0.3-point difference) and could plausibly fall within normal training noise for ImageNet-scale models, undermining the claim of "significant improvement."

The abstract/discussion claims that Hermite, Fourier, and Tropical activations all "significantly improve" over GELU/ReLU baselines, but Table 1 shows Fourier actually underperforms the GELU baseline on ConvNeXt-T (81.91% vs 82.04% top-1, 95.77% vs 96.01% top-5), which directly contradicts this overarching claim.

No comparison against other learnable-activation baselines discussed at length in the related work (e.g., Padé/rational activations, Snake, learnable Swish, spline-based KAN variants); the only baseline is static GELU, which is a weak comparison for establishing competitiveness of the proposed methods.

No wall-clock time or actual training throughput comparisons are reported despite the paper explicitly discussing FLOPs/memory overhead concerns—this omission makes it hard to judge whether the accuracy/perplexity gains justify the computational cost in practice.

The tropical activation, one of the three headline contributions, lacks the paper's core theoretical contribution (closed-form variance-preserving initialization); the authors state the second-moment calculation is deferred to "a later work" and coefficients are initialized ad hoc to all ones, making this component feel underdeveloped relative to the Hermite/Fourier treatment.

The polynomial-mapping proposition (Prop 3.32, degree grows as d^L with depth) is a fairly straightforward inductive result with limited novel insight or practical implication, adding bulk to the theoretical contribution without much payoff.

No empirical verification of the theoretical variance-preservation claims (e.g., no plots of measured activation/gradient variance across layers during training) despite this being the central motivating mechanism of the paper.

Scale of experiments (ConvNeXt-T 28M, GPT-2 124M) is modest by current standards for a paper claiming viability in "large-scale" tasks, and only one model size per architecture is tested, limiting evidence for scalability claims.

Substantial portions of the paper (Section 5 discussion of wavelets, complex-valued interpretations, bio-plausibility, and the KAN "digression" appendix) are speculative asides not tied to concrete experiments, diluting focus from the core empirical contribution.

strengths: Provides a rigorous, closed-form variance-preserving initialization scheme for learnable orthogonal-basis activations (Hermite, Fourier), extending He et al.'s analysis in a mathematically clean way that avoids the 'fit-to-classical-activation' trick needed for rational activations (Yang & Wang, 2024).

Demonstrates learnable polynomial/trigonometric/tropical activations at a considerably larger scale than most prior learnable-activation or KAN-related work (ConvNeXt-T on full ImageNet-1k, GPT-2 124M on OpenWebText), which is a meaningful step beyond the common MNIST-scale demonstrations criticized in the related work section.
Nice theoretical connection extending Zhang et al.'s tropical-geometry view of ReLU networks to show that polynomially activated deep networks are themselves multivariate polynomial mappings.

Careful and useful practical engineering discussion: numerical stability of Hermite polynomial evaluation via recursion/log-gamma reformulation, custom CUDA kernels, FLOPs/memory complexity analysis, and guidance on Lagrange vs. Hermite interpolation when fitting classical activations.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (degree, initialization scheme, learnability of coefficients, clamping) that isolate the contribution of each design choice.
Extensive, well-organized related-work coverage situating the contribution against KAN, rational activations, tropical geometry, and polynomial neural network literature.
weaknesses: Empirical gains are inconsistent and often marginal: Fourier activation actually underperforms the GELU baseline on ImageNet-1k (81.91/95.77 vs. 82.04/96.01), and Tropical activation's top-5 accuracy is also worse than baseline (95.90 vs. 96.01), which contradicts the abstract's claim of 'significantly improve[d]' accuracy across the board.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported; single-run results with differences on the order of 0.1-0.3% (vision) make it hard to assess whether the reported improvements are meaningful or within noise.

The paper's own theoretical framework (variance-preserving initialization via closed-form second moments) explicitly does not cover the tropical activation, since its second-order moment calculation is deferred to future work — this weakens the coherence of presenting tropical activations as a first-class contribution alongside Hermite/Fourier.

No direct empirical comparison against the closest related method (Pade/rational activations, Yang & Wang 2024) or against KAN variants, despite extensive discussion of both in related work; the paper only compares against static GELU baselines.
Only a single model size is tested per domain (ConvNeXt-T, GPT-2-124M), with no scaling experiments to verify whether the observed (often small) benefits persist or grow at larger scale.
No wall-clock/runtime benchmarks are provided despite a detailed theoretical FLOPs/memory analysis, leaving the practical efficiency trade-offs unverified empirically.

The polynomial-mapping proposition (network composition of polynomial activations yields a polynomial mapping) is a straightforward induction with limited demonstrated practical implication beyond restating known ideas from prior tropical/polynomial network literature.

strengths: Introduces a principled variance-preserving initialization scheme for learnable activations based on orthonormal bases (Hermite, Fourier), with closed-form second-moment expressions and rigorous proofs (Appendices C-E), improving on prior rational-activation approaches that lacked closed-form moments.

Unlike much of the learnable-activation/KAN literature that relies on small-scale datasets like MNIST, this work validates its claims on genuinely large-scale tasks: GPT-2 (124M) on OpenWebText and ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet-1k, which is a meaningful strength and directly addressed in the related-work critique of prior papers.

Provides a formal proof (Appendix F) that polynomially-activated deep networks correspond to multivariate polynomial mappings, connecting to prior tropical-geometry interpretations of ReLU networks (Zhang et al. 2018).
Extensive and well-organized ablation studies (degree, initialization scheme, learnability of coefficients, clamping) that isolate the contribution of each proposed component.
Practical engineering contributions: efficient recursive Hermite computation reducing complexity from O(d^2) to O(d), custom CUDA kernels, and a released library, improving reproducibility.

The Hermite/Lagrange interpolation-based fine-tuning strategy for adapting pretrained models (matching function and derivative) is a novel and practically useful idea, with a supporting CIFAR-10 fine-tuning experiment.
Multiple seeds (3) with reported mean ± standard error across all major experiments, and honest reporting of inconclusive results (e.g., CIFAR-10 Fourier/Tropical) rather than only favorable ones.
weaknesses: Reported improvements over GELU/SiLU baselines on ImageNet and OpenWebText are often small and appear to fall within or near the reported standard-error bars (e.g., ConvNeXt-T Top-1: 82.18±0.13 for Hermite vs 82.01±0.04 for GELU), raising doubts about the statistical significance of the main empirical claims.

Significant training-time overhead (30-90% slower per the Limitations section) is a substantial practical cost that is not adequately weighed against the marginal accuracy gains in the main results section.

The tropical activation's variance-preserving proof (Theorem 3.19/Appendix E) is informal and relies on an asymptotic approximation argument (n→∞) rather than a rigorous derivation comparable to the Hermite/Fourier proofs.

No direct empirical comparison against the rational-activation baseline (Yang and Wang 2024) that the paper explicitly positions itself against in the introduction, despite claiming to solve the closed-form second-moment problem that motivated that prior work.

The theoretical framework assumes the pre-activation signal follows a specific fixed distribution (normal/uniform) at every layer, but this is only approximately true in practice as distributions evolve through depth; the paper does not empirically verify how well this assumption holds in the trained networks.

Experiments are limited to a single model scale per task (GPT-2 124M, ConvNeXt-T); no evidence is given on whether the benefits (or overhead) scale favorably to larger models, which is important for claims about "large-scale learning tasks."

The core novelty relative to closely related prior work on Hermite/Chebyshev activations (Lokhande et al. 2020; Nebioglu and Iliev 2023) is incremental, primarily the initialization scheme, though this is acknowledged and contextualized reasonably well in related work.
Fine-tuning and CIFAR-10 experiments, while illustrative, are relatively small-scale and could be seen as secondary evidence rather than strong independent validation.

strengths: Rigorous, self-contained theoretical derivations of variance-preserving initialization for Hermite, Fourier, and Tropical activation families, avoiding the curve-fitting trick used by prior rational-activation work (Yang & Wang, 2024) via closed-form second-moment computation from orthonormality.

Reasonably broad empirical scope: experiments on both a vision backbone (ConvNeXt-T/ImageNet-1k) and a language model (GPT-2/OpenWebText), plus CIFAR-10 pretraining/finetuning and toy 2D decision-boundary visualizations.

Multiple ablations (degree, initialization scheme, learnability of coefficients, clamping) performed with 3 seeds and reported mean±std, which is good experimental hygiene relative to many activation-function papers.

Practical engineering contributions: recursive Hermite formulation reducing FLOPs/memory from O(d^2) to O(d), parallel CUDA kernels, and an amplitude-phase reformulation of the Fourier activation to reduce cost.

Interesting conceptual framing connecting polynomial-activated networks to multivariate polynomial mappings and tropical activations to discrete convex conjugates, with a thorough literature review including a useful critical discussion of KAN and Kolmogorov-Arnold theory.
weaknesses: The headline empirical gains are marginal and often within noise: on ImageNet (Table 1), Hermite's Top-1 gain over GELU (82.18 vs 82.01) is smaller than its own reported std (0.127), and Fourier/Tropical are frequently no better or worse than the GELU baseline (e.g., Fourier has lower Top-5 than GELU, Tropical has worse train loss). The paper's own CIFAR-10 section admits Fourier/Tropical results are 'inconclusive.'

The claimed efficiency benefit is contradicted by the Limitations section, which reports 30-90% slower training on GPU—this directly undercuts the abstract's claim of 'opens the door for improving the efficiency of large-scale learning tasks,' and the added FLOPs for Fourier (88.69G vs 87.52G) and Tropical are non-trivial despite claims of negligible overhead.

No direct empirical comparison against the closest prior work it explicitly targets (rational/Padé activations of Yang & Wang 2024, Molina et al. 2019 Safe-Padé), despite extensive conceptual discussion of why the proposed method should be preferable; without a head-to-head experiment, the central claim that 'rational functions are unnecessary' is not substantiated quantitatively.

The multivariate-polynomial-mapping proof (Appendix F, Prop. F.3) is a straightforward induction showing composition of polynomials remains polynomial—mathematically correct but not a particularly deep or novel result, despite being listed as a primary contribution.

Statistical rigor is limited: only 3 seeds are used throughout, and many reported improvements have overlapping error bars/standard errors, making it hard to assess whether observed differences are meaningful rather than noise, especially for GPT-2 where SiLU shows anomalously poor performance relative to GELU baseline, raising questions about hyperparameter tuning fairness across activations.

Ablations (Tables 3-6) are only conducted on the vision task; no equivalent ablation study is provided for the language modeling task, limiting generality of conclusions about degree, initialization, and learnability choices.
The clamping ablation (Table 6) shows negligible difference with/without clamping, undermining the claim that eliminating clamping mechanisms is a meaningful contribution.

The paper is dense with tangential material (extended KAN discussion, wavelet/complex-valued speculation in the Discussion) that dilutes focus from the core empirical claims, while the core results are comparatively thin and inconsistent across the three proposed activation families.
The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not engage with any specific considerations.

strengths: Provides a clean theoretical framework for variance-preserving initialization of learnable activations built on orthonormal bases (Hermite, Fourier), yielding closed-form forward/backward gain formulas that avoid the curve-fitting trick previously needed for rational activations (Yang and Wang, 2024).
Introduces a novel tropical polynomial activation with an elegant interpretation as a discrete convex conjugate / generalization of ReLU, along with its own variance-preserving initialization proof.

Empirical validation goes beyond toy datasets: experiments on large-scale tasks (ConvNeXt-T on ImageNet-1k, GPT-2 124M on OpenWebText) with multiple seeds and reported variance, which is uncommon and valuable in the learnable-activation literature that the paper itself critiques for over-relying on MNIST.

Solid theoretical contribution proving that polynomially activated deep networks are multivariate polynomial mappings (Appendix F), connecting to prior tropical-geometry views of ReLU networks (Zhang et al. 2018).
Thorough ablation studies (degree, initialization scheme, learnability of coefficients, clamping) that isolate the contribution of each design choice.
Practical/engineering contribution: efficient recursive Hermite kernel reducing complexity from O(d^2) to O(d), and a released library, aiding reproducibility.

Interesting and useful fine-tuning application via Hermite interpolation to match pretrained activations (GELU) while preserving derivative information, demonstrated with a CIFAR-10 transfer experiment.
Extensive and well-organized related work, including a thoughtful critical discussion of KAN and the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem's actual relevance to such networks.
weaknesses: Overall performance gains on the large-scale benchmarks are often marginal and sometimes within noise: e.g., Hermite improves ImageNet-1k Top-1 by only ~0.17pp over GELU, and Fourier actually underperforms GELU (81.82 vs 82.01 Top-1, 95.73 vs 95.95 Top-5), undermining claims that these activations "exceed" traditional ones across the board.

Reported numbers are inconsistent between tables for the same configuration (e.g., Hermite degree 3 achieves 82.18% in Table 1 but 82.34% in Table 3's ablation), raising concerns about result stability/reproducibility and reducing confidence in the significance of reported improvements.

The CIFAR-10 experiment shows very high variance for Fourier (91.5 ± 1.3), making it impossible to draw confident conclusions about whether Fourier truly outperforms GELU there, yet the abstract/discussion imply general superiority.

No direct empirical comparison against the rational activation baseline (Yang and Wang, 2024) that motivated this work, despite claiming the orthogonal-basis approach 'solves' its initialization problem — a head-to-head comparison would substantiate the claimed advantage.

The paper acknowledges 30-90% slower training due to the new activations but only reports FLOPs, not wall-clock times, making it hard to assess real-world practicality of the proposed method despite the stated efficiency motivation.

Claims such as demonstrating improvements 'for the first time' over ReLU/GELU at scale are somewhat overstated given the modest and inconsistent effect sizes; the significance/impact of the contribution would benefit from more conservative framing.
The decision boundary visualizations (Sec 4.2, Appendix M) are only qualitative illustrations on toy 2D datasets and do not provide rigorous quantitative insight beyond visual intuition.

Limited discussion of when/why Fourier activation underperforms compared to Hermite and Tropical, despite having the highest FLOPs/parameter cost among the proposed methods (43 vs 13 vs 19 FLOPs/Act in Table 1), which is an important trade-off left unexplored.
